analysis.one_liner: Extends do-not-call protections to every phone user and lets more people sue robocallers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the federal Do Not Call rules so they cover all telephone subscribers, not just people with home landlines. It would also remove the rule that currently lets a company make one unwanted call per year without penalty, and it would broaden the private right of action, letting more people sue callers who break the rules. The Federal Communications Commission would have 270 days after passage to update its regulations.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone, especially the growing share of households with only cellphones, who today get less protection under Do Not Call rules written for residential landlines. People pestered by repeated unwanted sales calls would gain a clearer legal right to sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cellphone users and anyone tired of sales calls

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the word 'residential' from the Do Not Call provisions of the Communications Act, so the registry and its protections cover all telephone subscribers rather than only residential lines [S2].

Removes the allowance for 'more than one telephone call within any 12-month period' by the same entity, so a single unwanted call would count as a violation instead of companies getting one free call a year [S2].

Expands the private right of action for calls that violate the Do Not Call rules, strengthening ordinary people's ability to sue telemarketers in court rather than relying solely on government enforcement [S2].
Requires the FCC to revise its regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement the expanded protections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies, lead generators, and debt collectors that rely on cold-calling would face compliance costs, the loss of the one-call-per-year allowance, and greater exposure to lawsuits. The modest government cost is the FCC's work to rewrite its rules within 270 days.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost and overreach for legitimate callers: appointment reminders, fundraiser calls, and small businesses doing outreach could face liability for a first call, since the bill removes the one-call-per-year grace period [S2].

Expanding the private right of action invites more litigation, including suits that critics of the Telephone Consumer Protection Act argue are filed by plaintiffs' attorneys over technical violations rather than genuine consumer harm [S2].
Scammers who make illegal robocalls are often overseas and hard to serve or collect from, so stronger legal tools may punish domestic businesses more than they deter the worst callers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary people is real but modest in dollar terms: fewer unwanted calls and a clearer right to sue. The costs fall on telemarketing businesses and would raise the risk of litigation over first-time calls. On balance this is a consumer-protection bill with limited downside for the public, but its impact is narrower than its title suggests because the worst robocallers are often unreachable by lawsuits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2024 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and it sat there until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on March 20, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S4].
On March 22, 2024, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, the furthest it ever progressed [S4].
The bill drew one cosponsor, a Democrat [S3].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketing and cold-calling businesses keep the current rules, including the one-call-per-year allowance and a private right of action limited to residential subscribers. Phone users gained nothing.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce and never reported it back or scheduled action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor action during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the single cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee never moved the bill; the record shows no Republican support.

industries.note: The bill removes their one-call-per-year allowance, extends do-not-call protections to cellphone-only subscribers, and expands their exposure to private lawsuits. Its failure preserves the status quo under which these firms may call any subscriber once a year without penalty [S2].

industries.industry: Debt collectors and customer outreach callers
industries.note: Broadened liability for a first unwanted call would raise compliance and litigation costs for any business that relies on outbound calling.
